title: Backlogs, timeboxes, dashboards, release map and project canvas
blurb: Define the PRINCE2 Agile key terms on sight: backlogs, benefit, dashboards, epic, project canvas, release map, timebox and waterfall.
question: A new board member wants a one-page visual summary of why the project is worth doing, and asks where to see release status and burn charts between meetings. Which two artifacts should the project manager point to?

teach.h: A shared vocabulary for agile projects
teach.body: PRINCE2 and agile grew up separately, so they share no common terminology. PRINCE2 Agile therefore mixes both sets of terms. The Foundation syllabus expects you to define eight of them from the Glossary: backlog (project and product), benefit, dashboard (project and team), epic user story, project canvas, release map, timebox (iteration, release and stage) and waterfall. Most of them are agile artifacts that replace or tailor a familiar PRINCE2 management product.
teach.cite: PRINCE2 Agile V2 book 5.8 and Glossary; syllabus 1.3.1

head: PRINCE2 management product
PRINCE2 Agile artifact
teach.caption: Each practice keeps its PRINCE2 purpose; the artifact is simply the agile form of the product.
A backlog is a prioritized list of requirements for a product, made of (epic) user stories or other formats (Glossary, 8.3.2.1).
Dashboards are pulled, not pushed: people look when they need to, instead of waiting for a report (Table 12.1, 12.3.2.1).

levels.label: Stage
levels.sub: Authorized by the board one at a time

teach.caption: A timebox is a fixed period: the end date holds and the content flexes. PRINCE2 Agile names three levels (Glossary).

teach.body: An epic user story is a large or vague story that breaks down into more detailed stories (8.3.2.2). A benefit is the measurable improvement from an outcome that the investing organization sees as an advantage; an output, such as a new app, is never itself a benefit. Waterfall is linear, sequential delivery: each phase finishes before the next starts, so it cannot adapt during the process (2.2).

teach.h: The project canvas: eight elements on one page
items: Users and scope (the project product, epics and main features).
Benefits (expected, measurable, with tolerance) and major risks.
It is a one-page visual business justification that tailors or replaces the business case (6.3.2.1).

teach.caption: The release map clusters user stories into releases and serves as both project plan and stage plan (8.3.2.5, 8.4.4).

teach.body: Project manager Amara Okafor is briefing a new board member on the digital membership project. She shows the project canvas as the one-page case for the investment, and the release map with two releases of three iterations each. The chief product owner keeps the project backlog of epics; the app team's product owner runs its product backlog. Between meetings, the board member can pull release status and burn charts from the project dashboard, while Amara pulls team detail from the team dashboard.

teach.text: Do not swap the pairs. The PROJECT backlog holds epics, replaces the project product description and belongs to the CPO; a PRODUCT backlog belongs to one team's product owner and links the team DoD. The TEAM dashboard replaces the checkpoint report; the PROJECT dashboard replaces the highlight and end stage reports.

items: Backlog: a prioritized list of requirements. Project backlog (epics, CPO) and product backlog (stories, PO).
Benefit: a measurable improvement seen as an advantage; outputs are not benefits.
Team dashboard = checkpoint report; project dashboard = highlight and end stage reports.
Epic: a large or vague story that breaks into detailed stories.
Project canvas: one-page business justification with eight elements.
Release map: releases of usually two to four iterations; it is the project and stage plan.
Timebox levels: iteration, release, stage. Waterfall: linear and sequential.

summary: You can now define each PRINCE2 Agile key term and say which management product it replaces. You can also tell the project and product backlogs, and the team and project dashboards, apart.

A.q: Which term describes a large or vague user story that is broken down into more detailed user stories?
A.why: An epic is a large or vague user story that breaks down into more detailed user stories (book 8.3.2.2).

whyNot.0: A persona is a fictional, needs-based profile of a user, not a requirement to be split.
whyNot.2: A story map arranges user activities in order and breaks them into stories; it is a planning technique, not the large story itself.
whyNot.3: An acceptance criterion is a condition a story must meet to be accepted, not a large story.

A.q: Which PRINCE2 Agile artifact replaces the checkpoint report?
A.why: The team dashboard replaces the checkpoint report. It is updated in team planning and retrospective workshops and the project manager pulls information from it (Table 12.1).

whyNot.0: The project dashboard replaces the highlight report and the end stage report, not the checkpoint report.
whyNot.1: The release map replaces the project plan and stage plan.
whyNot.3: The daily log is kept as it is in PRINCE2 Agile; it is the project manager's diary, not a team progress report.

A.q: What are the three levels of timebox named in PRINCE2 Agile?
A.why: The Glossary names three timebox levels: iteration, release and stage.

whyNot.1: Sprint and increment are Scrum terms and phase is not a PRINCE2 Agile timebox level; PRINCE2 Agile uses iteration as the generic word for a sprint.
whyNot.2: A task is not a timebox level, and the list leaves out the stage.
whyNot.3: A day is not one of the three levels, and the project is not a timebox level; the stage is.

B.q: Which statement about the project backlog is correct?
options: It is owned by each team's product owner
It replaces the stage plan for each stage
It holds the team's tasks for one iteration
It replaces the project product description
B.why: The project backlog is the PRINCE2 Agile tailoring that replaces the project product description; it holds mostly epic user stories (8.3.2.1).

whyNot.0: The chief product owner owns the project backlog; each product owner owns a team's product backlog.
whyNot.1: The release map replaces the stage plan (and the project plan).
whyNot.2: Task-level detail for the next iteration sits in the team plan, not the project backlog.

B.q:
Which two statements about a benefit are correct?
1. It is a measurable improvement resulting from an outcome.
2. It is seen as an advantage by the investing organization.
3. It is a specialist product handed over by a delivery team.
4. It is the same thing as a release delivered to users.
B.why: The Glossary defines a benefit as a measurable improvement resulting from an outcome, perceived as an advantage by the investing organization (statements 1 and 2).

whyNot.1: Statement 3 describes an output (a specialist product), and an output is not a benefit.
whyNot.2: Statement 4 is wrong: a release delivers outputs; the benefit is the measurable improvement that follows.
whyNot.3: Both 3 and 4 describe outputs or their delivery, not benefits.

B.q: A board member wants to check release status, burn charts and current risks without waiting for a report. Which artifact should they pull this from?
B.why: The project dashboard replaces the highlight report; it shows release status, burn charts, current risks and issues, and the board pulls information from it (12.3.2.1, Table 12.1).

whyNot.0: The team dashboard holds team-level progress and is pulled by the project manager, not the board.
whyNot.2: The project canvas is the one-page business justification, not a progress view.
whyNot.3: The risk register records risks and their status, but not release status or burn charts.

options: A list of epics that replaces the project product description
A one-page summary that replaces the business case
A visual plan of releases used as the project and stage plan
A team-level plan of tasks for the next iteration
C.why: The release map clusters user stories into releases (usually two to four iterations each) and represents both the project plan and the stage plan (8.3.2.5, 8.4.4).

whyNot.3: That describes the team plan, produced when a team accepts a work package.

C.q:
Identify the missing words in the following sentence.
A [?] is a one-page visual business justification covering vision, business value, options, costs, users, scope, benefits and major risks.
C.why: The project canvas holds those eight elements on one page and tailors or replaces the business case (Glossary, 6.3.2.1).

whyNot.0: The release map is a plan of releases and features, not a business justification.
whyNot.1: The project brief is a separate product used to authorize initiation; it is not the one-page canvas.
whyNot.2: The project dashboard is a progress view for the board, not a business justification.

C.q: How does PRINCE2 Agile describe waterfall delivery?
options: Linear and sequential, each phase finished before the next
Iterative, with a release every two to four iterations
Timeboxed, with scope flexed inside each stage
Flow-based, pulling new work when capacity allows
C.why: Waterfall is linear and sequential: each phase is completed before the next begins, and its main limitation is that it cannot adapt during the process (2.2, Glossary).

whyNot.1: Regular releases of a few iterations describe iterative-incremental (agile) delivery, not waterfall.
whyNot.2: Timeboxing with flexed scope is an agile technique, the opposite of a fixed sequential plan.
whyNot.3: Pulling work as capacity allows describes Kanban flow, not waterfall.

reteach.title: Match each old product to its agile twin
reteach.question: If you already know PRINCE2 management products, which agile artifact takes each one's place?

blocks.body: Think of each term as a PRINCE2 product in agile clothing. The business case becomes a one-page project canvas. Plans become a release map. The project product description becomes the project backlog of epics; product descriptions become a team's product backlog. Reports become dashboards that people pull: the team dashboard for the project manager, the project dashboard for the board.

blocks.text: Timebox levels are iteration, release and stage. A sprint is the Scrum name for an iteration, not a separate PRINCE2 Agile level.

explain.body: A backlog is a prioritized list of requirements. The project backlog holds mostly epics, replaces the project product description and is owned by the chief product owner. Each team's product backlog holds detailed user stories, links the team DoD and is owned by that team's product owner.

test.q: Who owns the product backlog for a delivery team?
test.why: The product owner owns the team's product backlog and keeps it aligned with the project backlog (Table B.1).

whyNot.0: The chief product owner owns the project backlog and sets priorities across teams.
whyNot.2: The team coach helps the team self-manage and facilitates workshops; it does not own a backlog.
whyNot.3: The project manager agrees work packages with product owners but does not own their backlogs.

explain.body: The team dashboard replaces the checkpoint report and is updated and reviewed in team planning and retrospective workshops; the project manager pulls from it. The project dashboard replaces the highlight and end stage reports and is reviewed in progress review workshops; the board pulls from it.

test.q: Where is the team dashboard updated and reviewed?
options: Progress review workshops with the board
Release planning workshops at stage ends
The project initiation and closure workshops
test.why: Table 12.1: the team dashboard is updated and reviewed during team planning and retrospective workshops.

whyNot.0: Progress review workshops update and review the project dashboard.
whyNot.1: Release planning workshops update the release map and team OKRs at stage boundaries.
whyNot.3: The project initiation workshop agrees approaches, the project DoR and DoD and the high-level release map, and the closure workshop ends the project; neither is where the team dashboard is kept up to date.

explain.body: A timebox is a fixed period at one of three levels: iteration, release or stage. The release map shows how many releases there will be, when, and which features each holds. A release usually spans two to four iterations.

test.q: A release usually contains how many iterations?
test.why: A release map groups user stories into releases, each usually two to four iterations long (8.3.2.5).

whyNot.0: A single iteration is the smallest timebox; a release usually groups several.
whyNot.2: Five to eight is longer than the usual release length.
whyNot.3: Ten to twelve iterations would be far longer than a usual release.

explain.body: The project canvas is a one-page visual business justification with eight elements. A benefit is a measurable improvement seen as an advantage by the investing organization. Waterfall is linear and sequential, with each phase finished before the next, so it cannot adapt mid-process.

explain.caption: Waterfall: one pass, each phase complete before the next.

test.q: What is the main limitation of waterfall delivery noted in PRINCE2 Agile?
options: It does not allow adaptability during the process
It cannot produce a business case or plans
It requires several teams working in parallel
It replaces stages with fixed-length iterations
test.why: The book notes that waterfall's main limitation is that it does not allow adaptability during the process (2.2).

whyNot.1: Waterfall projects can and do have business cases and plans.
whyNot.2: Waterfall does not depend on parallel teams; that is a scaling question.
whyNot.3: Iterations are an agile timebox; waterfall runs phases in sequence instead.
